items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a factor that makes an issue happen or makes it worse”?
items.answer: Cause
items.markingKey: Cause: a factor that makes an issue happen or makes it worse. [1]

items.stem: Give two different causes of the use of economic sanctions. For each, say whether it is a political, economic, social, technological or environmental factor.
items.answer: States want a response to aggression that stops short of war (political); A government violates international law or human rights (political).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each cause; 1 mark each correct type [4]

items.stem: Identify two causes of the export of plastic waste to poorer countries and state what type of factor each one is.
items.answer: Weak enforcement of waste rules in receiving countries (political); Consumers in rich countries use large amounts of single-use plastic (social).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each cause; 1 mark each correct type [4]

items.stem: Felix finds this paragraph in an online article: “The spread of online disinformation during elections has many roots. Platform algorithms promote content that attracts strong emotional reactions. In addition, many users share posts without checking their source. Some experts also point out that laws on election advertising were written before social media existed. As a result, voters make choices based on false information.” Identify two causes of the issue given in the source.
items.answer: Any two of: Platform algorithms promote content that attracts strong emotional reactions; many users share posts without checking their source; laws on election advertising were written before social media existed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Amara finds this paragraph in an online article: “The export of plastic waste to poorer countries has many roots. Recycling at home is more expensive than shipping waste abroad. In addition, consumers in rich countries use large amounts of single-use plastic. Some experts also point out that weak enforcement of waste rules in receiving countries. As a result, air and water pollution near recycling sites.” (a) State whether “recycling at home is more expensive than shipping waste abroad” is mainly a political, economic, social, technological or environmental cause. (b) Suggest one further cause of the issue that is not mentioned in the source.
items.answer: (a) Economic. (b) Mixed plastics are hard to recycle.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark relevant cause; 1 mark brief explanation [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that data protection laws do not cover new technologies clearly is the most important cause of state use of facial recognition surveillance. You may wish to consider: the quality of evidence; local, national and global factors.
items.answer: For: This political factor directly shapes the issue. It links to the consequence: people may avoid protests for fear of being identified. Against: Other causes also matter: the cost of cameras and computing power has fallen sharply; governments face pressure to prevent crime and terrorism. Causes interact, so ranking them depends on the country and the evidence available. Judgement: A supported judgement weighs the evidence for each cause and recognises that they interact.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by “cause” in Global Perspectives?
options: A factor that makes an issue happen or makes it worse.
A long-term condition that makes an issue likely to develop.
One of several causes that together produce an issue.
A relationship in which two things change together, which does not by itself prove that one causes the other.
items.answer: A factor that makes an issue happen or makes it worse.
items.markingKey: Cause: a factor that makes an issue happen or makes it worse. [1]

items.stem: Identify two causes of low voter turnout among young people and state what type of factor each one is.
items.answer: Voting procedures, such as having to vote in person on a working day, are inconvenient (political); Many young people move home often, so they are not registered at their current address (political).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each cause; 1 mark each correct type [4]

items.stem: A survey asked 200 people in Valdoria to choose the main cause of the spread of online disinformation during elections. Results: “Political advertising online is cheap and can be targeted at small groups”: 24; “Many users share posts without checking their source”: 38; “Laws on election advertising were written before social media existed”: 76; other reasons: 62. Calculate the percentage of respondents who chose the most popular cause.
items.answer: 38% chose “Laws on election advertising were written before social media existed”.
items.markingKey: Most popular = 76; 76/200 × 100 = 38%. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Chloe finds this paragraph in an online article: “Low voter turnout among young people has many roots. Young people feel that political parties ignore issues that matter to them. In addition, low trust in politicians after high-profile scandals. Some experts also point out that many young people move home often, so they are not registered at their current address. As a result, politicians focus policies on older voters who turn out in higher numbers.” (a) Identify one consequence mentioned in the source. (b) Explain which cause in the source a government could most easily address.
items.answer: (a) Politicians focus policies on older voters who turn out in higher numbers. (b) The national government could act on causes it controls, e.g. by deciding to make voting compulsory, with a small fine for non-voters; causes linked to attitudes or global markets are harder to change.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark choice; 1 mark explains why within government control; 1 mark comparison with a harder cause [3]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that many young people move home often, so they are not registered at their current address is the most important cause of low voter turnout among young people? Consider different perspectives in your answer. You may wish to consider: underlying and immediate causes; the quality of evidence.
items.answer: For: This political factor directly shapes the issue. It links to the consequence: politicians focus policies on older voters who turn out in higher numbers. Against: Other causes also matter: young people feel that political parties ignore issues that matter to them; voting procedures, such as having to vote in person on a working day, are inconvenient. Causes interact, so ranking them depends on the country and the evidence available. Judgement: A supported judgement weighs the evidence for each cause and recognises that they interact.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “an effect or result of an issue or of a course of action”?
items.answer: Consequence
items.markingKey: Consequence: an effect or result of an issue or of a course of action. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A consequence can be large in scale but low in severity. Reason (R): Scale measures how many are affected, while severity measures how seriously they are affected. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Both true; R explains A. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Unintended consequences only follow bad policies. Reason (R): Even well-designed policies can change behaviour in unexpected ways. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false; R is true. [1]

items.stem: The table shows how many people are affected by corruption in public procurement in three countries. Country | Population (millions) | People affected (thousands). Calvania | 60 | 6,000. Marvona | 12 | 2,400. Lunaria | 25 | 1,250. Calculate the percentage of the population of Marvona that is affected.
items.markingKey: 2,400 thousand ÷ 12 million = 2,400 ÷ 12,000; × 100 = 20%. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Omar, a student in Cape Town, is investigating migration caused by climate change after noticing families in a coastal village moving inland after repeated flooding. (a) Identify one short-term and one long-term consequence of the issue. (b) Identify one stakeholder affected by the issue and describe how they are affected.
items.answer: (a) Short-term: Pressure on housing and services in the cities that receive migrants. Long-term: Loss of culture and identity for communities that must relocate. (b) The government of a low-lying Pacific island state: its territory may become uninhabitable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark stakeholder; 1 mark effect [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the national consequences of the under-representation of women in parliaments are more serious than its global consequences.
items.answer: For: Policies on issues such as childcare and violence against women receive less attention: this is felt directly by people’s lives. Local and national effects are immediate and visible. Against: Global consequences such as A country scores poorly in international gender equality rankings affect many more people. Global effects can be long-term and harder to reverse. Judgement: Seriousness depends on the criteria used (scale, severity, duration, reversibility); a supported judgement weighs these.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Using two consequences of the under-representation of women in parliaments, explain the difference between the scale and the severity of a consequence.
items.answer: Scale is how widely an effect is felt; severity is how serious it is for those affected. “Fewer female role models for girls considering politics” is local in scale; “Parliaments are seen as less legitimate by half the population” is national in scale, but either could be more severe depending on how harmful and lasting it is for the people affected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark scale defined; 1 mark severity defined; 1 mark each consequence used correctly [4]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Some consequences of an issue can be positive. Reason (R): Every global issue harms all stakeholders equally. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is true, but R is false.
items.markingKey: A true (e.g. remittances from migrants); R false. [1]

items.stem: A report from Bogotá describes false rumours about polling station closures shared in a community messaging group. The issue is part of a wider debate about the spread of online disinformation during elections. Identify one short-term and one long-term consequence of the issue.
items.answer: Short-term: Voters make choices based on false information. Long-term: Trust in election results and in the media falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Sofia, a student in Karachi, is investigating the export of plastic waste to poorer countries after noticing open burning of imported plastic near a recycling yard, causing breathing problems for nearby residents. (a) Identify one short-term and one long-term consequence of the issue. (b) Explain which consequence is likely to be the most severe.
items.answer: (a) Short-term: Air and water pollution near recycling sites. Long-term: Health problems for informal waste workers. (b) For example, “Health problems for informal waste workers”, because it is long-lasting and difficult to reverse; others may affect more people but less seriously.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark choice; 1 mark severity criterion (duration/irreversibility/vulnerability); 1 mark comparison [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a proposed response to an issue, saying who should do what”?
items.answer: Course of action
items.markingKey: Course of action: a proposed response to an issue, saying who should do what. [1]

items.stem: Ines suggests that, to address reform of the UN Security Council, the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities. Explain one strength and one weakness of this course of action.
items.answer: Advantage: it would stop one country blocking action to prevent genocide. Limitation: the permanent members would have to agree, and they can veto Charter amendments.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark developed; 1 mark limitation, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Yusuf suggests that, to address migration caused by climate change, the national government should create planned relocation schemes within countries. Explain one strength and one weakness of this course of action.
items.answer: Advantage: moves can be organised safely before disaster strikes. Limitation: communities may resist leaving ancestral land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark developed; 1 mark limitation, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Two courses of action are proposed to address the use of economic sanctions. Action 1: the UN Security Council should allow humanitarian exemptions for food and medicine. Action 2: the UN Security Council or regional bodies should use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms. Suggest one criterion, other than cost, that should be used to compare the two actions, and explain why it matters.
items.answer: Effectiveness/acceptability/feasibility/speed: e.g. acceptability matters because an action that stakeholders oppose may be blocked or ignored.
items.markingKey: 1 mark criterion; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: A team scored three courses of action to address the use of economic sanctions from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion (for cost, 5 = cheapest). Action | effectiveness (weight 2) | cost (weight 1) | acceptability (weight 2) | speed of impact (weight 1). P: use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms | 5 | 1 | 5 | 2. Q: combine sanctions with diplomacy and clear conditions for lifting them | 1 | 4 | 1 | 3. R: allow humanitarian exemptions for food and medicine | 5 | 3 | 3 | 3. Calculate the weighted total for each action and identify which the team should recommend.
items.answer: P: 5×2 + 1×1 + 5×2 + 2×1 = 23; Q: 1×2 + 4×1 + 1×2 + 3×1 = 11; R: 5×2 + 3×1 + 3×2 + 3×1 = 22. Recommend P (use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms).
items.markingKey: 1 mark method (score × weight, summed); 1 mark all totals correct; 1 mark correct recommendation [3]

items.stem: Two courses of action are proposed to address the use of economic sanctions. Action 1: the UN Security Council or regional bodies should use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms. Action 2: the UN Security Council should allow humanitarian exemptions for food and medicine. (a) Explain one advantage of Action 1. (b) Suggest one criterion, other than cost, that should be used to compare the two actions, and explain why it matters.
items.answer: (a) They aim at decision-makers rather than the whole population. (b) Effectiveness/acceptability/feasibility/speed: e.g. acceptability matters because an action that stakeholders oppose may be blocked or ignored.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark advantage; 1 mark developed [2] (b) 1 mark criterion; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the best way to address the export of plastic waste to poorer countries is for the exporting governments to ban exports and build domestic recycling capacity. You may wish to consider: acceptability to stakeholders; effectiveness; feasibility.
items.answer: For: Countries take responsibility for their own waste. It acts on a cause of the issue: recycling at home is more expensive than shipping waste abroad. Against: It is costly and takes time. An alternative is to tighten international rules on plastic waste trade: the 2019 Basel amendments require consent before contaminated plastic waste is shipped. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Assess the claim that the best way to address migration caused by climate change is for the national government to create planned relocation schemes within countries.
items.answer: For: Moves can be organised safely before disaster strikes. It acts on a cause of the issue: rising sea levels threaten low-lying islands and deltas. Against: Communities may resist leaving ancestral land. An alternative is to extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change: it would give displaced people clear legal rights. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “how practical a course of action is, given cost, time, resources and political support”?
items.answer: Feasibility
items.markingKey: Feasibility: how practical a course of action is, given cost, time, resources and political support. [1]

items.stem: Priya suggests that, to address lowering the voting age to 16, the local government should lower the voting age to 16 for local elections first. Explain one strength and one weakness of this course of action.
items.answer: Advantage: its effects can be tested before national change. Limitation: young people may see it as a token gesture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark developed; 1 mark limitation, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Explain why the national government is an appropriate actor to make voting compulsory, with a small fine for non-voters.
items.answer: The national government has the authority, resources or reach to carry it out; turnout in Australia, where voting has been compulsory since 1924, is regularly above 90%.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies power/authority; 1 mark links to the action [2]

items.stem: Two courses of action are proposed to address low voter turnout among young people. Action 1: the education ministry should run citizenship education programmes in schools. Action 2: the electoral commission should introduce automatic voter registration. Explain one advantage of Action 1.
items.answer: It builds knowledge and the habit of participation early.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the best way to address corruption in public procurement is for the national government to publish all public contracts online (open contracting)? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: Citizens, journalists and rival firms can spot suspicious deals. It acts on a cause of the issue: officials have wide discretion and little oversight when awarding contracts. Against: Publication alone does not punish anyone. An alternative is to create an independent anti-corruption agency with powers to prosecute: it can investigate powerful officials without political interference. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: “The best way to address the use of economic sanctions is for the UN Security Council to allow humanitarian exemptions for food and medicine.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: unintended consequences; acceptability to stakeholders.
items.answer: For: They reduce harm to civilians. It acts on a cause of the issue: states want a response to aggression that stops short of war. Against: Banks may still refuse payments to avoid risk. An alternative is to use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms: they aim at decision-makers rather than the whole population. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a long-term condition that makes an issue likely to develop”?
items.answer: Underlying cause
items.markingKey: Underlying cause: a long-term condition that makes an issue likely to develop. [1]

items.stem: Give two different causes of low voter turnout among young people. For each, say whether it is a political, economic, social, technological or environmental factor.
items.answer: Low trust in politicians after high-profile scandals (social); Voting procedures, such as having to vote in person on a working day, are inconvenient (political).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each cause; 1 mark each correct type [4]

items.stem: Explain why it is difficult to identify a single cause of corruption in public procurement.
items.answer: The issue has several interacting causes, for example contract information is not published, so citizens cannot check it and public sector pay is low compared with the value of the contracts officials control; they operate at different levels (local, national, global) and reinforce each other, and a correlation between one factor and the issue does not prove it is the main cause.
items.markingKey: 1 mark several causes identified; 1 mark explains interaction / different levels; 1 mark correlation ≠ causation or need for evidence [3]

items.stem: Diego finds this paragraph in an online article: “The under-representation of women in parliaments has many roots. Women carry more unpaid caring work, leaving less time for politics. In addition, women politicians face more online abuse. Some experts also point out that cultural stereotypes that leadership is a male role. As a result, policies on issues such as childcare and violence against women receive less attention.” Suggest one further cause of the issue that is not mentioned in the source.
items.answer: Parties choose men for safe seats more often than women.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relevant cause; 1 mark brief explanation [2]

items.stem: A survey asked 500 people in Halvoria to choose the main cause of reform of the UN Security Council. Results: “Any change to the UN Charter can be vetoed by the permanent members”: 80; “The Council’s structure reflects the balance of power in 1945”: 95; “Regional rivals disagree about which countries should get new seats”: 190; other reasons: 135. Calculate the percentage of respondents who chose the most popular cause. Explain why this result does not prove that this is the main cause of the issue.
items.answer: 38% chose “Regional rivals disagree about which countries should get new seats”. The survey measures opinion, not causation; respondents may lack expertise, and the sample may not be representative.
items.markingKey: Most popular = 190; 190/500 × 100 = 38%. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer; 1 mark opinion ≠ evidence of cause; 1 mark sample/representativeness or expertise point [4]

items.stem: Assess the claim that poorer countries lack funds to build flood defences is the most important cause of migration caused by climate change. You may wish to consider: local, national and global factors; underlying and immediate causes.
items.answer: For: This economic factor directly shapes the issue. It links to the consequence: pressure on housing and services in the cities that receive migrants. Against: Other causes also matter: rising sea levels threaten low-lying islands and deltas; repeated droughts destroy the livelihoods of farmers. Causes interact, so ranking them depends on the country and the evidence available. Judgement: A supported judgement weighs the evidence for each cause and recognises that they interact.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “how widely a consequence is felt: the number of people or the size of the area affected”?
items.answer: Scale
items.markingKey: Scale: how widely a consequence is felt: the number of people or the size of the area affected. [1]

items.stem: Using two consequences of threats to press freedom, explain the difference between the scale and the severity of a consequence.
items.answer: Scale is how widely an effect is felt; severity is how serious it is for those affected. “Citizens rely on social media rumours rather than verified news” is local in scale; “International criticism and possible sanctions” is global in scale, but either could be more severe depending on how harmful and lasting it is for the people affected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark scale defined; 1 mark severity defined; 1 mark each consequence used correctly [4]

items.stem: Using two consequences of the use of economic sanctions, explain the difference between the scale and the severity of a consequence.
items.answer: Scale is how widely an effect is felt; severity is how serious it is for those affected. “Pressure on the targeted government to negotiate” is global in scale; “Shortages and price rises for ordinary citizens” is national in scale, but either could be more severe depending on how harmful and lasting it is for the people affected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark scale defined; 1 mark severity defined; 1 mark each consequence used correctly [4]

items.stem: Read this extract from a community newsletter in Mumbai: “Residents are concerned about farmers downstream noticing lower river levels during the dry season.” Identify one short-term and one long-term consequence of the issue.
items.answer: Short-term: Diplomatic tension and threats between neighbouring states. Long-term: Electricity for millions of people in the upstream country.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: The table shows how many people are affected by threats to press freedom in three countries. Country | Population (millions) | People affected (thousands). Jovania | 40 | 4,000. Lunaria | 2 | 300. Loristan | 60 | 4,800. Calculate the percentage of each population affected. Identify the country where the issue is largest in scale and the country where it is most severe in proportion to population.
items.answer: Jovania: 4,000 ÷ 40,000 × 100 = 10%; Lunaria: 300 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 15%; Loristan: 4,800 ÷ 60,000 × 100 = 8%. Largest scale: Loristan (4,800 thousand). Highest proportion: Lunaria (15%).
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark all three percentages; 1 mark largest absolute number; 1 mark highest proportion [4]

items.stem: Jonas argues that the national consequences of the under-representation of women in parliaments are more serious than its global consequences. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: Policies on issues such as childcare and violence against women receive less attention: this is felt directly by people’s lives. Local and national effects are immediate and visible. Against: Global consequences such as A country scores poorly in international gender equality rankings affect many more people. Global effects can be long-term and harder to reverse. Judgement: Seriousness depends on the criteria used (scale, severity, duration, reversibility); a supported judgement weighs these.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by “course of action” in Global Perspectives?
options: A proposed response to an issue, saying who should do what.
How practical a course of action is, given cost, time, resources and political support.
How far a course of action would actually reduce the issue.
Comparing the expected costs of an action with its expected benefits.
items.answer: A proposed response to an issue, saying who should do what.
items.markingKey: Course of action: a proposed response to an issue, saying who should do what. [1]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one limitation of the proposal that the United Nations member states should extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change.
items.answer: Advantage: it would give displaced people clear legal rights. Limitation: many states fear it would commit them to accepting very large numbers of people.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark developed; 1 mark limitation, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Explain why the dam operator is an appropriate actor to share real-time data on dam filling and river flows.
items.answer: The dam operator has the authority, resources or reach to carry it out; downstream countries can plan ahead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies power/authority; 1 mark links to the action [2]

items.stem: A team scored three courses of action to address the spread of online disinformation during elections from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion (for cost, 5 = cheapest). Action | effectiveness (weight 2) | cost (weight 2) | acceptability (weight 1) | speed of impact (weight 1). P: require platforms to label and remove false political content | 1 | 1 | 5 | 2. Q: fund independent fact-checking organisations | 4 | 3 | 5 | 5. R: teach media literacy in schools | 3 | 2 | 3 | 4. Calculate the weighted total for each action and identify which the team should recommend.
items.answer: P: 1×2 + 1×2 + 5×1 + 2×1 = 11; Q: 4×2 + 3×2 + 5×1 + 5×1 = 24; R: 3×2 + 2×2 + 3×1 + 4×1 = 17. Recommend Q (fund independent fact-checking organisations).
items.markingKey: 1 mark method (score × weight, summed); 1 mark all totals correct; 1 mark correct recommendation [3]

items.stem: Two courses of action are proposed to address reform of the UN Security Council. Action 1: the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities. Action 2: the UN member states should add new permanent members such as the G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan) and African states. Suggest one criterion, other than cost, that should be used to compare the two actions, and explain why it matters.
items.answer: Effectiveness/acceptability/feasibility/speed: e.g. acceptability matters because an action that stakeholders oppose may be blocked or ignored.
items.markingKey: 1 mark criterion; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: A team scored three courses of action to address disputes over shared rivers from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion (for cost, 5 = cheapest). Action | effectiveness (weight 4) | cost (weight 2) | acceptability (weight 1) | speed of impact (weight 1). P: negotiate a basin-wide water-sharing treaty | 5 | 4 | 5 | 3. Q: ask a neutral mediator such as the African Union or the World Bank to help | 4 | 5 | 5 | 4. R: share real-time data on dam filling and river flows | 5 | 3 | 4 | 1. Calculate the weighted total for each action and identify which the team should recommend.
items.answer: P: 5×4 + 4×2 + 5×1 + 3×1 = 36; Q: 4×4 + 5×2 + 5×1 + 4×1 = 35; R: 5×4 + 3×2 + 4×1 + 1×1 = 31. Recommend P (negotiate a basin-wide water-sharing treaty).
items.markingKey: 1 mark method (score × weight, summed); 1 mark all totals correct; 1 mark correct recommendation [3]

items.stem: Assess the claim that the best way to address threats to press freedom is for the government and philanthropists to fund public-interest journalism through independent trusts. You may wish to consider: feasibility; effectiveness.
items.answer: For: It supports reporting that the market will not pay for. It acts on a cause of the issue: governments want to control criticism before elections. Against: Funders may try to influence content. An alternative is to protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws: it allows investigative journalism to hold power to account. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Assess the claim that the best way to address threats to press freedom is for the parliament to protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws. You may wish to consider: unintended consequences; acceptability to stakeholders; effectiveness.
items.answer: For: It allows investigative journalism to hold power to account. It acts on a cause of the issue: governments want to control criticism before elections. Against: Governments say some restrictions are needed during emergencies. An alternative is to fund public-interest journalism through independent trusts: it supports reporting that the market will not pay for. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a short-term event that sets off an issue whose underlying causes already exist”?
items.answer: Trigger
items.markingKey: Trigger: a short-term event that sets off an issue whose underlying causes already exist. [1]

items.stem: Give two different causes of migration caused by climate change. For each, say whether it is a political, economic, social, technological or environmental factor.
items.answer: Rising sea levels threaten low-lying islands and deltas (environmental); Poorer countries lack funds to build flood defences (economic).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each cause; 1 mark each correct type [4]

items.stem: Tariq claims that weak enforcement of waste rules in receiving countries is “the cause” of the export of plastic waste to poorer countries. Explain why this claim is too simple.
items.answer: The issue has several interacting causes, for example weak enforcement of waste rules in receiving countries and consumers in rich countries use large amounts of single-use plastic; they operate at different levels (local, national, global) and reinforce each other, and a correlation between one factor and the issue does not prove it is the main cause.
items.markingKey: 1 mark several causes identified; 1 mark explains interaction / different levels; 1 mark correlation ≠ causation or need for evidence [3]

items.stem: A survey asked 800 people in Loristan to choose the main cause of migration caused by climate change. Results: “Weak international agreements on reducing emissions”: 128; “Poorer countries lack funds to build flood defences”: 96; “Repeated droughts destroy the livelihoods of farmers”: 248; other reasons: 328. Calculate the percentage of respondents who chose the most popular cause.
items.answer: 31% chose “Repeated droughts destroy the livelihoods of farmers”.
items.markingKey: Most popular = 248; 248/800 × 100 = 31%. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Priya finds this paragraph in an online article: “Lowering the voting age to 16 has many roots. 16-year-olds can already work and pay tax in many countries. In addition, youth campaign groups have become better organised. Some experts also point out that political parties hope to gain young voters’ support. As a result, A larger electorate that includes people still at school.” (a) State whether “16-year-olds can already work and pay tax in many countries” is mainly a political, economic, social, technological or environmental cause. (b) Explain which cause in the source a government could most easily address.
items.answer: (a) Economic. (b) The parliament could act on causes it controls, e.g. by deciding to lower the voting age to 16 for all elections; causes linked to attitudes or global markets are harder to change.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark choice; 1 mark explains why within government control; 1 mark comparison with a harder cause [3]

items.stem: Amara argues that any change to the UN Charter can be vetoed by the permanent members is the most important cause of reform of the UN Security Council. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: This political factor directly shapes the issue. It links to the consequence: the Council fails to act on some humanitarian crises because of a veto. Against: Other causes also matter: the Council’s structure reflects the balance of power in 1945; regional rivals disagree about which countries should get new seats. Causes interact, so ranking them depends on the country and the evidence available. Judgement: A supported judgement weighs the evidence for each cause and recognises that they interact.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “how serious a consequence is for those affected, for example how harmful, lasting or irreversible it is”?
items.answer: Severity
items.markingKey: Severity: how serious a consequence is for those affected, for example how harmful, lasting or irreversible it is. [1]

items.stem: Suppose the parliament decides to protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws. Explain one limitation or possible unintended consequence of this action.
items.answer: For example: governments say some restrictions are needed during emergencies. Such effects are not the aim of the action but could reduce its benefit or create new problems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark plausible unintended outcome; 1 mark explains why it is unintended/its effect [2]

items.stem: Using two consequences of reform of the UN Security Council, explain the difference between the scale and the severity of a consequence.
items.answer: Scale is how widely an effect is felt; severity is how serious it is for those affected. “States act outside the UN, through regional alliances” is global in scale; “Countries in Africa feel under-represented, reducing the UN’s legitimacy” is global in scale, but either could be more severe depending on how harmful and lasting it is for the people affected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark scale defined; 1 mark severity defined; 1 mark each consequence used correctly [4]

items.stem: The table shows how many people are affected by corruption in public procurement in three countries. Country | Population (millions) | People affected (thousands). Fendaria | 4 | 480. Pelora | 12 | 360. Jovania | 4 | 320. Calculate the percentage of the population of Fendaria that is affected.
items.markingKey: 480 thousand ÷ 4 million = 480 ÷ 4,000; × 100 = 12%. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: A report from Lima describes families in a coastal village moving inland after repeated flooding. The issue is part of a wider debate about migration caused by climate change. (a) Identify one short-term and one long-term consequence of the issue. (b) Suggest one positive consequence that some stakeholders might experience.
items.answer: (a) Short-term: Pressure on housing and services in the cities that receive migrants. Long-term: Loss of culture and identity for communities that must relocate. (b) Some groups may benefit, e.g. UNHCR if it must work within the mandate states have given it; or new jobs or pressure for reform.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark plausible positive consequence; 1 mark who benefits [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the local consequences of disputes over shared rivers are more serious than its global consequences? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: Reduced water for irrigation downstream: this is felt directly by people’s lives. Local and national effects are immediate and visible. Against: Global consequences such as diplomatic tension and threats between neighbouring states affect many more people. Global effects can be long-term and harder to reverse. Judgement: Seriousness depends on the criteria used (scale, severity, duration, reversibility); a supported judgement weighs these.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by “feasibility” in Global Perspectives?
options: How far stakeholders are willing to support a course of action.
How practical a course of action is, given cost, time, resources and political support.
A proposed response to an issue, saying who should do what.
Comparing the expected costs of an action with its expected benefits.
items.answer: How practical a course of action is, given cost, time, resources and political support.
items.markingKey: Feasibility: how practical a course of action is, given cost, time, resources and political support. [1]

items.stem: Tomás suggests that, to address reform of the UN Security Council, the UN member states should add new permanent members such as the G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan) and African states. Explain one strength and one weakness of this course of action.
items.answer: Advantage: it would make the Council more representative of today’s world. Limitation: regional rivals oppose specific candidates, so agreement is hard to reach.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark developed; 1 mark limitation, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Explain why the education ministry is an appropriate actor to run citizenship education programmes in schools.
items.answer: The education ministry has the authority, resources or reach to carry it out; it builds knowledge and the habit of participation early.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies power/authority; 1 mark links to the action [2]

items.stem: A team scored three courses of action to address low voter turnout among young people from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion (for cost, 5 = cheapest). Action | effectiveness (weight 3) | cost (weight 1) | acceptability (weight 1) | speed of impact (weight 2). P: make voting compulsory, with a small fine for non-voters | 4 | 1 | 4 | 5. Q: introduce automatic voter registration | 4 | 2 | 1 | 4. R: run citizenship education programmes in schools | 5 | 5 | 4 | 5. Calculate the weighted total for each action and identify which the team should recommend.
items.answer: P: 4×3 + 1×1 + 4×1 + 5×2 = 27; Q: 4×3 + 2×1 + 1×1 + 4×2 = 23; R: 5×3 + 5×1 + 4×1 + 5×2 = 34. Recommend R (run citizenship education programmes in schools).
items.markingKey: 1 mark method (score × weight, summed); 1 mark all totals correct; 1 mark correct recommendation [3]

items.stem: Two courses of action are proposed to address state use of facial recognition surveillance. Action 1: the parliament should allow it only with a court warrant and independent audits. Action 2: the exporting governments should restrict exports of surveillance technology to countries with poor human rights records. Explain one advantage of Action 1.
items.answer: It balances security with legal safeguards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: A team scored three courses of action to address the spread of online disinformation during elections from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion (for cost, 5 = cheapest). Action | effectiveness (weight 3) | cost (weight 1) | acceptability (weight 1) | speed of impact (weight 2). P: require platforms to label and remove false political content | 4 | 2 | 1 | 1. Q: fund independent fact-checking organisations | 4 | 2 | 3 | 1. R: teach media literacy in schools | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4. Calculate the weighted total for each action and identify which the team should recommend.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method (score × weight, summed); 1 mark all totals correct; 1 mark correct recommendation [3]

items.stem: Sofia argues that the best way to address lowering the voting age to 16 is for the education ministry to keep the age at 18 but improve citizenship education. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence. You may wish to consider: effectiveness; feasibility.
items.answer: For: It prepares young people before they vote. It acts on a cause of the issue: young people are affected by long-term decisions on climate and debt. Against: It does not give under-18s a voice now. An alternative is to lower the voting age to 16 for all elections: it gives a voice to people affected by long-term decisions. Judgement: A supported judgement compares actions on effectiveness, feasibility and acceptability, and may recommend a combination.
